answer:
According to the guidelines reviewed, direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) are preferred over warfarin in most patients with atrial fibrillation (AFib). This preference is explicitly stated as more suitable in "most eligible" patients. However, these recommendations are based on a CHA2DS2-VASc score which specifies patient eligibility for anticoagulation therapy. For patients who meet the specified criteria [Anticoagulation in Atrial Fibrillation (ACC/AHA/HRS), 2024], DOACs are strongly preferred over warfarin.

It's important to note that this preference holds true especially in most eligible patients, although not all AFib patients require anticoagulation. For different patient populations, the specific treatment recommendations can vary, so it is always best to consult guideline-based practices for personalized care [Anticoagulation with Direct Oral Anticoagulants (DOACs) in VTE Disease, ACCP, 2021]. 

Additionally, DOACs are also preferred over warfarin as first-line therapy for acute deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism without cancer. This recommendation is from another context which may not be directly comparable to the AFib treatment scenario but still provides relevant guidance [Antithrombotic Therapy for VTE Disease, ACCP, 2021]. 

Please consult with your professional healthcare provider to determine the best course of treatment based on individual patient characteristics and medical history.

results.content: Oral anticoagulation is recommended for patients with atrial fibrillation and a CHA2DS2-VASc score of 2 or more in men or 3 or more in women. Direct oral anticoagulants are preferred over warfarin in most eligible patients.

For acute deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism without cancer, direct oral anticoagulants are preferred over warfarin as first-line therapy. Anticoagulation duration is at least 3 months, extended indefinitely for unprovoked events with low bleeding risk.
results.source: ACCP Antithrombotic Therapy for VTE Guideline
results.citation: Antithrombotic Therapy for VTE Disease, ACCP, 2021
